etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English feeste, feste, borrowed from Old French feste, from Late Latin festa, from the plural of Latin festum (“holiday, festival, feast”), from Proto-Italic *fēs-tos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“god, godhead, deity”); see also Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god, goddess”). More at theo-. Doublet of fete, fiesta, and fest. Displaced Old English winhate.

definitions.definition: A very large meal, often of a ceremonial nature.
A festival; a holy day or holiday; a solemn, or more commonly, a joyous, anniversary.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 13:6:
quote.text: The seventh day shall be a feast to the Lord.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 2:41:
quote.text: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English feesten, festen, from Old French fester, from Medieval Latin festāre, from the noun. See above.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To partake in a feast, or large meal.

quote.citation: 1609, William Shakespeare, “Sonnet 47”, in Shake-speares Sonnets. […], London: By G[eorge] Eld for T[homas] T[horpe] and are to be sold by William Aspley, →OCLC:
quote.text: With my love's picture then my eye doth feast.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To hold a feast in honor of (someone).

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: He that shall see this day, and live old age,Will yearly on the vigil feast his neighborsAnd say “Tomorrow is Saint Crispian.”

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To serve as a feast for; to feed sumptuously.

quote.text: Or once a week, perhaps, for novelty / Reez'd bacon-soords shall feast his family.
